To understand dysfunctional, you first need to understand functional.

Something is functional when it works the way it is supposed to work. A functional car starts when you turn the key. A functional family supports its members, communicates openly, and handles problems in a healthy way. A functional team at work cooperates, divides tasks fairly, and gets things done.

Now, dysfunctional means the exact opposite: something that is supposed to work in a certain way, but doesn't — and this failure causes harm, pain, or serious problems.

It's not just "broken." It's broken in a way that hurts the people or things involved.
The Full Definition

Dysfunctional (adjective):

Describes a person, group, relationship, system, or organization that does not operate in a normal, healthy, or effective way, and as a result causes suffering, conflict, damage, or poor outcomes for those within it or affected by it.
Breaking It Down With Examples

1. A Dysfunctional Family

This is the most common use of the word. A dysfunctional family is one where the normal roles and behaviours of a healthy family are absent or twisted.

In a healthy family, parents protect their children, communicate honestly, set fair rules, and resolve conflict calmly. In a dysfunctional family, you might see:

  • A parent who abuses alcohol and becomes violent
  • Parents who constantly fight or manipulate each other
  • A child who is forced to take on adult responsibilities because the parents can't function
  • Emotional neglect, where nobody talks about feelings or problems

The key point: the family exists as a family, but it operates in a harmful, broken way. The damage shows up in the emotional and mental health of its members.

2. A Dysfunctional Relationship

Two people in a romantic or close relationship can be dysfunctional together. This means their patterns of behaviour toward each other are unhealthy and harmful — things like constant jealousy, emotional manipulation, dishonesty, poor communication, or cycles of breaking up and getting back together without resolving anything. The relationship functions in the sense that it continues to exist, but it doesn't function in the sense that it makes either person happy or healthier.

3. A Dysfunctional Organisation or Workplace

A workplace can be dysfunctional if, for example, managers bully employees, departments refuse to cooperate with each other, rules are unfair or inconsistently applied, or good people are punished while bad behaviour is rewarded. It is an environment that is supposed to be productive and fair, but is instead chaotic, toxic, or harmful.

4. A Dysfunctional System

You can call a system — like a country's healthcare system, a government, or a legal process — dysfunctional when it consistently fails to do what it was designed to do, often causing harm or injustice to the people it was meant to serve. For example: "The prison system is dysfunctional — it puts people behind bars but does little to prevent them from committing crimes again."
The Critical Nuance: It's Not Just "Broken"

This is very important. Dysfunctional does not simply mean broken or not working at all.

A car with a flat tyre is broken. But you wouldn't usually call it "dysfunctional." The word dysfunctional is used specifically for things that involve people, behaviour, relationships, or organised systems — things that have an intended healthy purpose — and where the failure is ongoing, rooted in behaviour or structure, and causes real harm.

Think of it this way:

  • A shattered window = broken
  • A family where a child is emotionally abused every day = dysfunctional

The word carries a weight of ongoing harm and deeply rooted problems, not just a one-time malfunction.
Degrees of Dysfunction

Dysfunctional exists on a spectrum. Something can be mildly dysfunctional (a workplace where communication is poor but nobody is being seriously harmed) or severely dysfunctional (a family torn apart by addiction, violence, or abuse). The word covers the whole range, but the context usually tells you how serious the dysfunction is.
What Dysfunctional Does NOT Mean

• It does not mean "completely destroyed." A dysfunctional family is still a family — it still exists — but it operates harmfully.
  • It does not mean "different from the norm" in a neutral sense. It specifically implies harm or serious failure.
  • It is not a casual word for minor inconveniences. Saying "my phone charger is dysfunctional" would sound odd to a native speaker — the word belongs to human systems, relationships, and social structures.
Common Collocations (Words It Often Appears With)

These are the phrases you will most often see or hear with "dysfunctional":

  • dysfunctional family ← by far the most common
  • dysfunctional relationship
  • dysfunctional system
  • dysfunctional organisation / workplace
  • dysfunctional behaviour
  • deeply dysfunctional (to emphasise severity)
  • highly dysfunctional
Synonyms (Similar Words)

• Broken (informal, less precise)
  • Troubled
  • Unhealthy (especially for relationships or families)
  • Toxic (emphasises the harm it causes to people)
  • Disordered
  • Malfunctioning (more mechanical, less human)

None of these are perfect substitutes. Dysfunctional is unique because it precisely captures the idea of a system or group that should work healthily but doesn't, causing harm.
Antonyms (Opposite Words)

• Functional — works as it should
  • Healthy — especially for families or relationships
  • Well-functioning
  • Stable
Example Sentences

1. She grew up in a deeply dysfunctional home, where her parents' constant arguments left her anxious and withdrawn.
  2. Many employees quit because the management style was dysfunctional — favourites were promoted regardless of performance.
  3. Experts argue that the country's immigration process is dysfunctional and in desperate need of reform.
  4. They had a dysfunctional relationship — they hurt each other constantly, yet couldn't seem to let go.
  5. He didn't realise how dysfunctional his childhood was until he became an adult and saw what healthy families looked like.
The One-Line Summary

Dysfunctional describes any person, group, relationship, or system that is supposed to work in a healthy, effective way — but instead operates in a harmful, broken, or chaotic way that causes real damage to those involved.
